title: I'm New To RPG Maker And Am Looking To Develop Something

posts.author: FayeOfBoops
posts.body:
Hey there, as the title says I'm pretty new to RPG Maker though I've been wanting to get into it for quite some time. Game Developing has always been an interest since I've been into creative writing for almost 20 years now.
I use RPG Maker MZ although I have MV too, and am simply curious if there's any tips of advice that could help me as I go? Also if there are any good tile sets or other useful resources that anyone can recommend - free or not - that would be wonderful!
Thanks,
Faye.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I have a few specific pieces of advice I can give (whether you follow them or not is up to you).
Learn Player Psychology
This isn't always easy (there are some outdated sources out there, or sources specific to certain types of games, so you have to be careful what you pick up.  Psychology behind someone playing a singleplayer game and someone playing an MMO are two VERY different things), but is necessary.  I suggest learning some sociology and psychology on top of stuff that's specific to game design.
Some of that stuff can be applied to PR, Advertising, and even building a community around your game.  It can also help you in dealing with criticism of your game or of yourself.
Create A Game Design Document
If you are serious about your game, before you even touch the Maker, I would create a Game Design Document.  These take many shapes and forms, but they are incredibly useful.  They will keep you from having scope creep, will keep you on track for the main themes in your game, and will help you organize things in your Database a lot better and ahead of time.
If you're just fiddling with the Maker, no need for one of these.  But, a serious attempt at making and completing a game, I always recommend you have a GDD.
Players Are Not Your Enemies
A lot of devs forget this along the way.  "They just want me to change my game to suit what they want!", "They just want me to sacrifice my vision!", "They don't understand what they're asking for!".  Some of this might be true... but more often than not... it isn't true in the slightest.
The minute you treat your players (or potential players) as an enemy, you have already failed to make a good game.
If a player hates your game, you will get two responses from them:
1.  An insult laden tirade with no specific examples or issues about why your game is bad.
2.  No response at all, they just don't play.
Any player that gives you feedback of any kind (I didn't like X because of Y), is a player who wants to help you succeed.  They aren't necessarily asking for you to do the thing they ask for.  They want what that change does.  "Game feels empty" isn't necessarily asking you to add 300 NPC's to an area or to fill a zone with 100 things to do.  It's asking for something else, and you get to figure out how to fix that problem (or even if you want to fix that problem to begin with).
If a player gives you feedback of any kind, it's because they care.  They want you to succeed as much as you want to succeed.
Never treat your players like an enemy.
No, not even in gameplay (positive reinforcement of doing something correct in the game is better than punishment for doing something wrong, in most cases, as an example).

posts.author: Deleted member 270061
posts.body: As Tai_MT said, have a vision for what you want to create and create a Game Design Document.  This will help you stay within in defined scope and keep you on track.  One of the things some developers have issues with is randomly coming up with "cool ideas" and the game loses focus.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
@Mac15001900
is right, and in basically any thread of "I am a beginner..." we have what might as well be considered our motto:
Start small and learn. Keep things simple.
No plugins, learn basic functions, and just have fun expiramenting with what the engine does out of the box.
Slowly increment up to bigger and bigger projects.
